name: Standard Route

pitch_detail.notes: Short committing moves onto the balanced summit block

rappels: 1 short (~20 ft) rappel from the fixed bolt on top of the block back to the ledge
descent_text: From the top of the balanced rock, most parties do not reverse the shoulder-stand/friction sequence (considered the route's real crux to downclimb) and instead rappel a single fixed bolt/chain anchor at the summit straight back down to the belay ledge - a short (~20 ft) single-strand rappel that any rope length easily covers. From the ledge, downclimb or step off to the talus/blocks at the base of the pillar. From there, descent is a reversal of the approach: regain the ridge crest and drop back toward Table Rock and the Sherpa-Argonaut basin, picking down through the boulder field and the Class 2-3 gully system - loose, rockfall-prone terrain where a helmet is strongly advised, and where parties note the unroped downclimb back to camp can take as long as the technical pitch itself, especially near dusk. Regain the climbers' boot path at the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction, re-ford Ingalls Creek, and climb back up and over Longs Pass to return to the trailhead. This is a single-pitch feature, so no multi-rappel sequence is needed for the balanced rock itself - the one bolted rappel off the top is the only roped descent on the Standard Route; parties climbing the broader Sherpa Peak West Ridge to reach the main summit (a separate, longer route) report needing several additional rappels off that ridge, but that is not part of this Standard Route's descent.
approach: Start at the Longs Pass Trailhead (Esmeralda TH) at the end of Teanaway River Road (USFS Rd 9737) out of the North Fork Teanaway. Take Longs Pass Trail #1229 climbing steadily through open pine forest and sagebrush switchbacks for about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft of gain (roughly 1.5-2 hours) to Longs Pass at approximately 6,200-6,400 ft, which opens up the first views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, and the Stuart Range crest. From the pass, drop off the north side on a steep, loose, eroded boot path (sometimes called the 'tapeworm') losing about 1,400-1,600 ft over roughly a mile to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft; this descent tread is dirt/scree and can be slick and hard on the knees. Ford Ingalls Creek (a rock-hop in low water, but a genuine wet crossing during early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it east/downstream about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at roughly 4,700 ft - the last dependable water source before the alpine basin above. From the junction, a climbers' boot path (referenced in trip reports as 'Variation #1' toward Mount Stuart) switchbacks up through forest and talus; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide separating two gullies, then drop into the eastern gully, which leads more directly toward Sherpa Peak. Class 2 slopes above the gully lead to 'Table Rock,' a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the boulder-choked Sherpa-Argonaut basin, a common high bivy for parties splitting the approach over two days. From Table Rock, a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the Stuart Range divide, putting climbers on the ridge crest east of the balanced rock; follow the crest west over blocks and sandy, exposed benches (Class 3-4) to reach the base of the balanced rock formation itself, where the Standard Route begins with a shoulder-stand or rope-lasso move to gain the east-side pedestal, then bolt-protected friction climbing (5.7) to the summit block. Car-to-base is roughly 6-7 miles one-way with roughly 6,000 ft of climbing on the way in, and Longs Pass to regain on the way out; expect loose rock and real route-finding through the gully/basin section, and carry all the water you'll need above the Beverly-Turnpike junction since the upper basin is dry.
overview: Sherpa Balanced Rock is a ~20-ft granite obelisk perched on the crest of Sherpa Peak (8,605-8,630 ft, figures vary), a satellite summit of Mt. Stuart in the Stuart Range, Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It sits about 100 yards from Sherpa's true western high point; a sight-level survey found the block only ~2 ft lower than that summit, so many climbers consider tagging the block the true top of the peak. Dave Mahre, with Gene and Bill Prater, made the first ascent in 1955. Reaching the flat top requires a short, bold, historically-protected sequence off an overhanging pedestal.
beta: This is less a 'route up the peak' than the technical crux feature of Sherpa Peak: a free-standing granite pillar near the true summit. Parties typically combine it with the Class 3-4 ridge traverse to Sherpa's main summit. The crux move onto the pedestal has historically been done either by shoulder-standing a partner or by throwing/lassoing a rope over the pedestal's point; from there, bolt-protected friction slab gains the flat top, from which a single aging bolt is used to rappel back down.
gear: Small selection of cams and nuts plus slings to back up the fixed pin
Sturdy approach shoes or light boots for the 3rd/4th-class ridge and gully
fa: Dave Mahre, Gene Prater, Bill Prater — 1955
face: East side (from the East Ridge crest)
